Not for me..... I was not expecting much, but for me, these bags are a joke. I can't believe so many are still available, but impossible to find out who actually makes them. I ordered the 45 piece set it comes with some serving pieces. As you will see in the photos, there were problems. Salad Forks, Dinner Forks, Knifes, Diner Spoons and teaspoons all had missing or smuggled flowers on the handles. I called Oneida customer service. They said they are not aware of the problems. I sent them the photos and they checked there stock and found the same problems. They told me to call Amazon and return the silverware. This set was made in Indonesia. I am hoping in a few months the problem will be fix. If you look at Macy's the reviews are the same thing. Since November 2022 there is this problem.  Oneida was sold to Lenox and Lenox was sold to someone else. The Molding/stamping has gone down hill.

Gimmicky and overpriced, the panini attachment costs the same as buying a panini press!. I got this because I toast bread, do waffles, poptarts- all sorts of stuff in the toaster on a regular basis so I figured I'd treat myself... SO it arrived and it's absolutely beautiful, the touchscreen is awesome and it's easy to use! That's the GOOD.

The bad is on waffles no matter what setting I use- it cooks them and leaves the edges kind of soft for some reason and the middle part is burnt. I don't know why but there's a round burnt ring on the middle that's about the size of a silver dollar- it burns it black too. The next bad thing on the waffle setting was to get the edges done I had to sometimes run the frozen waffle cycle 2 or 3 times. YES this thing cooks fast but when you factor in having to run it in there 2-3 times, not much time is really saved there.

I got about every bread this thing has an option for and the results for each weren't much better sadly. It was just MEH on each one. Didn't take my breath away at all and I truly expected a $400 toaster to be amazing! The truth is my $40 toaster does the same thing but better. A cheap toaster does what this does so you're paying for a fun fancy touch screen. Just get a cheap toaster and burn a few pieces if need be to find your perfect setting and write it down on a post-it to remember.

As far as the attachments- WAY overpriced. The panini attachment costs what a panini press would actually cost! $80 for a metal tray is insane! It probably cost them $2-$5 to manufacture that so it's highway robbery! But it's literally a metal-hinged tray your sandwich goes in. Cuisinart makes the GR-11 model and it's currently on Amazon for $59.99 and does a fantastic job! George Foreman has a panini press for $28 even! The point is why pay MORE for a little metal tray? You already paid the high price of $400 so why extort more money out of people? Accessories shouldn't be more expensive than an actual appliance. The whole idea is to be cheaper. That press shouldn't cost more than about $20. The warming tray costs $30 which is INSANE because you can buy a huge baking sheet for that! This is a tiny metal rack that sits on top of the toaster. Should cost like $10-15. My advice there is to just find a little metal rack and sit it on top of the toaster instead- use one of the wire ones as a baking sheet would trap heat in and hurt your appliance.

Bottom line? Overpriced gimmick with overpriced attachments. I know it says I get items for "free" so you'd wonder why I'm so pressed about the price but I will end up paying nearly $100 in taxes on this toaster and considering I have a nice 4 slot generic toaster that cooks more at once and does a better job that I paid $40 for, yeah I'm a little bitter about that! I'd honestly return this if that was an option for us.

Cosmetically-Challenged Nightlight/Clock With Awkward Setting Process, Dim Display. This PHILIPS AJH510/37 ALARM CLOCK is a decent night light--with four pretty, easily-changed colors to choose from--but not a particularly good choice for a bedside clock. At the highest brightness setting, the digital time readout is dim, and it's hard to see what time it is in the daytime. The night light (at the bottom of the clock) isn't exactly dim, but it doesn't provide much ambient light for the room--it serves mainly to show the clock's location. Certainly this nightlight/clock will not keep any sleeper awake!

The clock won't win any beauty contests, either. It's a mystery to me, why the manufacturer chose a battleship grey color for the fabric covering. Perhaps to suggest metal mesh? The grey background doesn't help the visibility of the dim orange readout at all. And the grey color doesn't harmonize well with the faux wood plastic disk atop the clock. The photo on the product page is fairly accurate regarding the clock's looks.

The clock's worst feature is the time and alarm-setting process. Depending on what you're trying to do, you must press a button or a location on the faux wood disc, and then fumble around with the volume control wheel to change the hours and minutes, type of alarm (buzzer or nature sounds), display brightness, etc. For me, the task of adjusting hours and minutes up and down, while holding the clock in hand and rolling a sideways-mounted wheel, is extremely awkward. Also, I found the pictorial "quick start" instructions hard to interpret when figuring out the alarm- and feature-setting process. The downloadable manual is similarly pictorial, but is slightly clearer.

At first, I was very confused by the "8UZ" setting, which was how I read the "BUZ" (for buzzer alarm) setting on the display. As for the buzzer alarm itself, it is one of those that starts with a soft beep and increases in volume and frequency until the sleeper wakes and stops it. (I like these.) However, at the very highest volume, the buzzer is probably not loud enough to wake a very sound sleeper.

As for the preloaded nature-sounds (and three music sounds), I listened to them all, but didn't like any except the "train" (railroad boxcars rolling past)--which is only appropriate for go-to-sleep use. (Go-to-sleep is one of the clock's features.) The nature sounds were probably recorded from nature, but they sound artificial. The music sounds include an "angelic harp" that I would quickly tire of, for either wake-up or go-to-sleep purposes.

Because of the ugly-duckling appearance, awkward setting process, and dim clock display, I rate this Philips AJH510/37 Alarm Clock at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Scary, Awkward-to-Use Grill Lacks On/Off Switch, Temperature Control. To only make grilled cheese sandwiches and panini, I thought this GEORGE FOREMAN 4-SERVING REMOVABLE PLATE GRILL AND PANINI PRESS (Black, GRP1060B) would be satisfactory for my needs. Wrong, wrong, wrong!

My grill arrived new in the box, and it didn’t smoke or smell bad when I followed the manufacturer’s instructions to start by heating it empty for 15 minutes (to burn off any manufacturing oil or residue). However, the budget-priced (about $29 on Amazon) grill is rather scary to use.

First, there is NO on/off switch or temperature control. The grill heats when you plug it in, and it gets VERY hot in about 5 minutes. You turn the grill off by unplugging it, and it takes quite a while to cool enough for you to remove the dishwasher-safe plates. At least the cord doesn’t heat up, and it doesn’t spark when you unplug it.

Second, the hinge, which “adjusts” to handle thicker or thinner items placed on the grill, is very clunky. When you open the lid and pull up, the hinge pulls up to make a wider space between the two grill plates. However, the hinge doesn’t pull evenly or all that easily.

Third, all of the black plastic parts (including the adjustable hinge) get hot when the grill is heated. You really need to handle this grill with oven mitts or hot pads.

Fourth, the electrical cord is extremely short--shorter than most “short cord” countertop appliances that use a short cord as a safety feature. Because the cord is so short, the cord won’t reach my kitchen countertop outlet unless I place the grill sideways on the countertop. This makes it awkward to load the grill, which is really designed to be opened from the front.

The worst of these four bad features is the lack of a temperature control. The only temperature is “very hot”, so it’s hard to toast grilled cheese sandwiches or panini sandwiches without burning them.

I wouldn’t dream of purchasing this grill for use in cooking meats or grilling vegetables. While the grill isn’t exactly flimsy, it is clear that the manufacturer has put the minimum amount of material into the grill’s manufacture. I’m pretty sure that the grill will burn out or quit working fairy soon if it is used at all regularly.

Fabulous Looks, But Overall Poor Design. This MR.COFFEE 12-CUP PROGRAMMABLE COFFEEMAKER, STAINLESS STEEL looks fabulous, brews fast, has easy-to-use buttons, includes a water filtration system, has a keep-warm plate, and includes a cleaning cycle setting. Unfortunately, the coffeemaker also has a hard-to-fill reservoir, a clumsy "removable filter basket", and an exposed showerhead-type water system that emits steam when the lid is opened.

The good looks are not enough to make me like this coffeemaker! Everything (coffee grounds and water) must be added from the top. This is all right when the coffeemaker is cold. However, if you open the top to add coffee for a second pot right after the first pot has brewed, the showerhead will send a cloud of steam straight into your face. (I strongly prefer a coffeemaker with an enclosed showerhead and a coffee basket that swings out sideways, like the slower-brewing [[ASIN:B0041A5H5S Hamilton Beach 12-Cup Digital Coffee Maker]].)

The lid on this Mr. Coffee coffeemaker has a second lid in the back half that flips up. I think this is intended for you to use in filling the reservoir, but the second lid doesn't always want to stay up. It's also faster to fill the reservoir by opening the entire lid. When you open the top, the entire mechanism with the showerhead feels flimsy, as if it will break easily (and early breakage has been my experience with this type of coffeemaker design).

The outer "removable filter basket" lacks a handle for easy removal. It has ear-like tabs that are hard to grip (especially if the coffeemaker is hot) and require using two hands to pull the basket up and out. If you're using the water filtration system, you will probably want to remove this outer basket for every pot, because you must put ground coffee (inside a paper or permanent filter) into the basket, and then place the water filtration system over the top of the basket. The water filtration system itself consists of a charcoal filter disk that slides into a frame or lid for the "removable filter basket".

The water filtration system is supposed to remove chlorine from your water, to make your coffee taste better. You need to change the charcoal filter every month. (The coffeemaker comes with just one filter.) This isn't very useful to me, because my tap water often tastes odd because of organic matter. Removing chlorine isn't enough, so I filter my coffee water with a different type of filter before adding it to the coffeemaker's water reservoir.

My coffeemaker arrived without either paper filters or the "Mr. Coffee nylon permanent filter" that is supposed to be included (according to the instructions). I guess that the permanent filter got removed in the warehouse, because the box wasn't completely sealed when it arrived. Some kind of additional filter is needed inside the "removable filter basket", or coffee grounds will escape into the carafe during brewing.

The coffeemaker comes with a short 26" cord, which is more or less standard for kitchen appliances now, especially heating appliances. The cord arrives coiled inside the coffeemaker's base, and needs to be pulled out when you first set up the coffeemaker.

Because of the many bad design features, I rate it this Mr. Coffee coffeemaker (Model BVMC-JPX37-AM) at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Cleans Pod Capsule Only; Does Not Eliminate Need for Descaling. These KEURIG 5000057588 K-CUP COFFEE MAKER RINSE PODS (10 Count, White) only clean your coffee maker’s pod capsule—they are NOT a substitute for regular descaling of your entire coffee maker (see [[ASIN:B00FOT9W5Q Keurig Descaling Solution]]). The rinse pods cleanse the pod area (where you place the pods) and the channel below, to prevent “flavour carryover” between brews—especially between cups of hot chocolate, apple cider, or fancy flavored coffees and cups of plain coffee or tea.

To use the rinse pods, you need to (1) insert a rinse pod and brew a cup with water; (2) remove the used rinse pod and discard the rinse water; (3) rinse the pod capsule by brewing another cup with water only; and (4) discard the rinse water. In practice, I needed to rinse the pod capsule twice, because the first rinse produced a cup of hot rinse water with a white ring of chemicals around the water surface.

I think it’s easier to rinse the pod capsule (to reduce flavour carryover) by brewing one cup of plain water and discarding the rinse water. Doing it that way also avoids adding mildly toxic chemicals to your coffee maker.

The rinse pods contain maltodextrin, sodium bicarbonate, citric acid, and sodium citrate. The warning on the box says “do not consume”; and, among other things, advises you to “Seek medical attention if a large amount is swallowed, if irritation persists, or if you feel unwell.”

Great Nonstick Finish, But NOT Dishwasher Safe; Pans Rust. Yes.. no.. maybe? (ultimately no).
Here are all my thoughts and observations, followed by my experience:

--It has a rotatable plug!! So if you go to plug it in and the prongs seem backward.. just turn it until it is the way you want it. Also allows you to plug it into a side ways receptacle and still be able to keep the unit upright. It can be a a little top heavy if your outlet isn't tight. Some outlets this feels firmly plugged in, and one of my other outlets is seems to back away from the wall a little. However, it still turns on and stays on.

--As expected from a UV-C bulb, it has a blue light emitting bulb. Don't stare at it. The bulb isn't exposed, but the light is still visible.

--Makes some noise when it is turned on. It isn't too loud (soft fan white noise), but it might be too loud for some depending where you put it.

--You will need to replace the bulb. Says it has MAX 5000 hours of life, so AT LEAST once per year. You know it is in need of replacement if the light is getting more dim, or better yet you can just make a plan to change it out every 6-8 months. No mention of where/how to buy replacements, though.

--Air is pulled into the closed system and it is with exposure to the light that the germs are annihilated. This does not sanitize/disinfect surfaces. It is strictly air borne. No filter as this type of purification doesn't require it. Depending on your needs, from what I have read using something like this along with a filter (hepa or electrostatic) type air purifier may make for best combo.

--The instructions say that, "it needs about 2 hours in 10 square meters of room" to start to gain benefit of disinfection. Small room, small space for best results (ie; 10'x10' room or less).

--From what I can surmise, this is for killing "airborne germs and odors".. so not for germs and such that have settled onto/into surfaces. It pulls air into through the cover, and from there the air and whatever is in it is exposed to the UV light HENCE why it will work best in smaller spaces. I do not know how much air it is able to pull through, or how far reaching it is. But closed, small rooms are likely to gain greatest and quickest benefit.

--Uses a UV-C bulb. "UV-C carries the most energy capable of destroying the bonds that hold together the DNA and RNA of viruses and bacteria, stopping them from working. The same sanitizing energy can also damage eyes and skin, and cause cancer". Do not stare at the bulb! Fortunately this bulb is covered and there is just a ring of light that can be detected. Even so, be mindful of not gazing at it.

--Ozone? UV illuminant: 253nm UV-C bulb ...at wavelengths shorter than 250 nanometres, they produce ozone, which is emitted out into the environment. So this just exceeds the threshold. Seems this is accurate in their saying that it does not emit ozone. Phew!

--VOCS? Information in packet alludes to it by stating, "If present in the environment, it will help eliminate formaldehyde" (which is an example of a VOC) So it may help in reducing off gassing from new products, or really old products, etc

--While a UV filter will not remove particulate matter, it can eliminate germs, bacteria, and viruses. As microorganisms in the air pass through the filter, UV rays will kill them. This ensures that common allergens and health-risks are eliminated in your home.

My experience?
Eh. No.

I have tried it in various areas: Trials 1-4 have too many variables to be able to determine if it is specifically this working. When it occurred to me to try option #5, I knew I had a winner, since it was one area that isn't getting air flow and it always has an off aroma, and I would be able to tell in short order if this is working or not. There would be nothing else to impact the way the room smelled. I would either smell the room or I wouldn't. So this is what /where I tried:

1. In our fully carpeted small bedroom where we sleep with our two big labs. (my large air purifier w/filter works, not sure about this. had it going for 6 hours prior to bed. No change. Unplugged it for sleep as the blue light illuminated the wall)

2. In a small room that has a couple of litter boxes set up. (Really couldn't tell)

3. In a small bathroom where we keep the door shut. It tends to have a weird smell in there despite being "clean". But it is still a lot of going in and out, and there is fluctuation of sense of weird smell. (can't tell for sure, but may consider this room for potential germ killing aspect anyway and use it for next 6-8 months)

4.. In a small area, near a litter box. The box is situated at the base of a set of stairs. While it is an open area, the air flow is stagnant. Curiously, shortly after plugging this in, I found the area to smell worse. I partly wonder if it was still early on and was actually pulling the odors out (therefor making it smell stronger?). I didn't see any fresh deposits made to the box. I didn't give it enough time to determine if it dissipates. I plugged my other definitely effective mini air purifier back in (non UV-C) and the air smelled cleaned up shortly after.
https://www.amazon.com/dp/B087JHKTRP/ref=pe_1098610_137716200_cm_rv_eml_rv0_dp

5. Final test location: In a small 10'x10' guest room where the door is always shut, and rarely opened. The room has an odd odor. Our house is old and really nothing has been updated since maybe the 70s, at least 30 years before my husband bought it right out of college, and we haven't done anything to it. I imagine there is off gassing from old wallpaper, carpet, furniture, etc. It isn't musty, it is just.. odd. Was really hoping to smell a change. I checked in at 2 hours (still smells) and again 4 hours later (still smells, no change - at all). At the time I am writing this, I still have it plugged in in that room. If I notice any spectacular change I will come back to edit.

So, not a product for me. The only other spot I could consider trying is in the kitchen area (maybe food smells?) IF I can find a spot to plug it in. Options are limited, so I likely won't make a spot for it. It is big and depending on your receptacle, it may take up two outlets.

There just isn't enough information about the product or the company to make me feel secure in this being an effective item. If I could have at least smelled the difference, then I would feel better. I see that there are a couple of other "companies" selling exact same model, which really isn't doing anything to increase my trust. However, if I experience anything different I will be back to update. Mixed reviews here, so maybe I missing something in my trials?

Editing my initial review (which is still below this revision), on September 16, 2013: So, the description here at Amazon for this vacuum has been changed from "NO MESS" to "LESS MESS." Much better description, as there is plenty of mess to clean up inside the vacuum dirt collection tray area. Also, a price drop, from $350 to $299.95. Over at Brookstone's Website, the "NO MESS" description has also been removed and changed to "Less Mess." I feel the fact the "NO MESS" description has been removed validates my original review. And I thank Brookstone for coming clean (no pun intended). And for those who accused me of lacking credibility with my review because it doesn't say "Amazon Verified Purchase," I'd like to reiterate here that I purchased this vacuum direct from Brookstone and not here at Amazon because at the time of purchase Brookstone had a coupon available, which lowered the price for me a bit. I still own and use the vacuum.

Original Review:

This vacuum (at $350) is so overpriced, it is insane.

First, let me warn you: Should your $350 Gtech Airram's battery ever fail, there is no way to use the vacuum. It would just be a brick. For that much money, they should allow, just as an emergency backup, the vacuum to be used with the charging cable plugged in. But no. If the battery is drained or dead, even with the cord plugged into it, the vacuum is useless.

But the above is not why I give this vacuum 2 stars.

They claim no mess? There is mess. In fact, you might need another vacuum to clean out the mess (dirt and dust and stuff vacuumed up) that accumulates into the collection area (even immediately after first use). Yes you will! (Yes, you can grab a cloth and wipe out all that dust. You will want to and have to. The video showing how the collection area has no mess, along with the written claims of same, are utter bs.)

I bought this vacuum direct from Brookstone, and am very disappointed. I really thought that for $350, there would be no mess (or at least, a tiny amount). One big complaint about bagless vacs is the mess in the collection areas. So, Gtech, in an effort to make the cost so high, claims "lightweight, clean, and cordless...no mess." It is lightweight. It is cordless. But it ain't clean. Not in the least. And there is mess.

So, if you got a lot of extra money to spend and you want cordless, light, and powerful, buy this vacuum. But do not expect clean. The only thing "clean" about this vac is that after you open up the cover, you're gonna have to CLEAN the inside.

To summarize: This vacuum is in no way worth $350, in my opinion...and you will have to clean the dust and dirt out of the collection area (with a rag or paper towels) just like you would with any bagless. There is mess and particles to manually empty seperate from what they call the "bales of dirt." Their so called "bales" after pulled out, stuff is still stuck to the underside of the cover, which you will have to pick out with your fingers. (This vacuum is not worth anything over $180, in my opinion.)

Positive: Convenient for quick touch ups since it is cordless. Light weight. Maneuvers fine. Seems to have good suction. Noise not too loud for me.

P.S. I doubt you would want this as a primary vacuum for your home. Better for quick touch-ups.

Another Love-Hate Relationship With A Dyson Vacuum. Should Be Different For Its High Price. I bought the V6 Absolute cheaper elsewhere, and not here via Amazon.

There are two suction levels: Low and Max. There is a remarkable difference between the suction power between the two. If you doubt this, simply attach the dust brush and hold it at the bottom of your shirt. On low, your shirt will not be held on by the suction. On Max, your shirt will be held onto the suction quite nicely, and as you'd expect.

I am extremely disappointed by the low suction power when the vacuum is not on the Max setting, I do not wanna use it. It just is not good enough. But on the vastly superior Max setting, you get a measly 6-minutes of battery power.

For its high price Dyson could have rectified this situation by designing the vac with a removable battery, and then include a second battery you can keep charged. When your 6 minutes are up, simply swap the second battery...putting the first battery into a charger.

Also, disappointingly, you cannot use this vacuum while the battery is being charged. This might have been a helpful feature if one ran out of battery after the 6 minutes but really needed to finish up a job right away.

For this whopping price, to only get 6 minutes using the desired Max suction setting is extremely upsetting to me. Again, I find the low setting suction level to be way to weak.

I realize battery technology is still limited...which is why I suggested they could have made this vacuum be able to swap out the battery, etc.

I do love the soft roller brush. I do love the handling of the vacuum. I do love the suction when it is on Max (and only on Max). Filter cleaning is easy. So, like I said, Love/Hate.

Again, this is a vacuum that they MSRP'd and originally sold it at their site for $599. Right now, as I write this review, they discounted it to $479.99. That is a lot of money for just 6 minutes of battery life for the suction I expect and the suction power I want. (And they could have easily fixed this situation by designing it with a swap-able battery, and including a second battery.)

On a side note: Hopefully one day Dyson will make a Cinetic cordless that has no filters to clean, just like with their wonderful Cinetic Big Ball Animal + Allergy. Once Dyson can give us a Cinetic Cordless with no filters to clean and more than 6 minutes of battery life on Max suction setting...my feelings will go from Love/Hate, to just Love.

Initial setup was fairly straightforward. After collecting several days worth of data I decided to delete them just because I was trying out features. I had to perform this seven times before the app would connect to the sensor again. I used the device for another week and suddenly it stopped collecting sleep data. For four days it sat under my mattress doing nothing. I tried contacting support and have not received a reply yet. An earlier question was answered fairly quick but I had to provide the serial number (adding a full day to the exchange) to get a simple data meaning question answered. On the fifth day the unit once again began sending data to the app. Is it defective? Perhaps. I'm unsure. But that leads me to my deepest concern. . .

It's supposed to be able to tell how long it takes you to fall asleep, when you're lightly or deeply asleep or in REM sleep as well as tracking when you snore, your pulse rate high, low and average through the night and how long it takes you to get up when you awake. Every night I go to bed early due to pain and will spend up to a few hours reading or watching video on my tablet. when the bar graph said I was lightly asleep, I wasn't. When it said I was deeply asleep, I wasn't. I have no idea how, without seeing my eye movement, it can know I'm in REM sleep. I think one time it said I took a while to get to sleep but most nights while I lay there reading it was logging it as some form of sleep and my falling asleep taking only a few minutes. I know I snore, my scouts once dragged me out of the tent because I was so loud, so I guess the snoring detector is accurate. It can also, some times, tell if you've taken a nap during the day and add that to the day's data though it appears there needs to be a susstantial time between getting up and going back for a nap otherwise the time gap gets logged as simply a really long interuption in your night's sleep. I tend to spend quite some time in bed on bad days and that seems to seriously confuse the device and app.
It's a slick idea, nothing to wear, nothing to start or stop manually. Just stuff it under your mattress as directed and hey presto, sleep data. F+ -->What was Bissell thinking?. I have a Bissell Spot Bot and I purchased a Bissell 9400 ProHeat 2X Select Upright Deep Carpet Cleaner for my boyfriend; both are superb products! However, I cannot phathom what Bissell was thinking when they produced this carpet cleaner. I tried it on an area of carpet that was only slightly dirty; but the results were very disappointing.

What they got right:
- Easy assembly
- Sleek vacuum design
- Useable power tools (power nozzle is good)
- Easy carry handle
- Excellent power cord holder
- Nice power cord release mechanism (no need to unwind cord from power cord wrap because you can just release the latch to drop the cord to the floor)
- Vacuum powers itself nicely along the carpet so there is hardly any pushing action required by the user

What they got terribly wrong:
- The soft PowerRoller doesn't clean; it's excellent on hardwood floors but that is not what this vacuum was designed for.
- The carpet does not dry in 30 minutes as stated UNLESS you hardly use any solution. Without using much solution, you might as well blow on the carpet with your mouth to try to dislodge the dirt because the results would probably be the same--which is no cleaning.
- The solution tank leaks around the cap when filled appropriately. I tried several times to reseal the cap but there was always some solution seepage.
- The dirty water collector tank also has water seepage even if you don't go above the fill line.
- I tried for 45 minutes to clean about a 6 x 7 area of carpet and it still looked as dirty as when I started. I then used the power tool and some elbow grease and tried again which gave me better results but still not good enough. My Bissell spot bot can clean the same area wonderfully but not this vacuum.
- By the time the hot water reaches the carpet it is either lukewarm or too cold to be of any cleaning use.

In summary, if the Bissell didn't leak all over, this vacuum would be excellent (but perhaps overkill) for cleaning a wood floor because the cleaning pad buffs up things nicely (I tried it my wood floor). However as a carpet cleaner, you would get better results by wetting a washcloth with warm water, applying some soap, getting down on your hands and knees and using some elbow grease to clean your carpet.

Barely does the job pitting cherries; although pits Bing cherries better. The purpose of this "industrial-sized" Leifheit cherry pitter is to be able to pit many cherries quickly without having to "reload" a cherry into the pitting chamber. I figured the need for a lot of pitted cherries when making pies or a large fruit salad would make such a gargantuan unit worthwhile. I already have the exceptionally designed and almost flawless [[ASIN:B000NQ925K OXO Good Grips Cherry Pitter]] but when this unit came became available, I felt it was worth trying out.

The unit comes with two rubber washers; one is a spare. What I had to do was remove the cardboard piece holding down the plunger arm and insert the rubber gasket into the slot. This gasket is needed to prevent the cherry pit from coming back into the cherry after I pulled up on the plunger. For my test, I tried to pit both the firmer Rainier cherries and the less firm Bing cherries with this cherry pitter. Even though the instructions do not mention pitting olives with this cherry stoner, I decided to try small black Kalamata olives as well--since my other cherry pitter can pit soft olives like this.

I loaded the Rainier cherries into the hopper and they didn't really line up in the pitting chamber; sometimes they had to be pushed into the hole for pitting. Once I pushed the plunger, I had to pull up fully to release the pitted cherry into the exit shoot. Of about 50 Rainer cherries I pitted many were damaged on the exit (partially squished or broken) and all but about 4 had the pits remain in the cherry. For the cherries that exited into the waiting bowl, I had to pry open the cherry to remove the pits. I then tried pitting about 50 sweet cherries and they pitted easier since they were softer cherries. However, I still had some squished cherries exit the hopper and about 6 of the cherries that exited had pits that had to be pulled out by hand. Since I also wanted to know if olives would work, I tried about 4 of them and found out quickly this unit cannot pit olives.

As I was washing the unit I noted that the washer was destroyed just from pitting these few cherries. It appears the plunger not only pitted my cherries but also chopped out part of the washer. When I inserted the washer, I made sure it was centered and that the pitter blade passed cleanly through the center of the washer's hole. However, with all the cherry pitting activity it probably moved around and caused large holes in the washer. Not only does this reduce the effectiveness of the pitting but I had to throw out the washer and put in the spare.

In summary, I cannot recommend this cherry pitter to anyone. The only redeeming quality it has are the rubber feet on the bottom of the unit that keeps the cherry pitter base firmly in place during pitting. Other than this, the unit is too huge. The pitting chamber so enormous compared to the hopper you put the cherries in. Also the plunger cannot be locked down for storage and stands at attention like a rocket about to take off. The pitter barely pits Bing cherries (the dark colored ones with a firm but softer flesh) and has a 95% failure rate when pitting Rainier cherries. I had high hopes for this cherry stoner and was sadly disappointed. I was going to give this unit 1 star but since it did pit the Bing cherries somewhat, I rated this 2 stars. I have not decided yet whether I'm going to send this to the recycling bin or keep it as a conversation piece, but I doubt I'll ever use this to pit cherries again.

This pepper mill needs improvement. This pepper mill is not only for wealthy consumers looking for another way to spend their money. It can be a medical aid in some cases for those with hand problems. I have no objection to a high-priced automatic pepper mill because those who have hand problems (arthritis, carpel tunnel, one arm or hand, etc.) will find it possible to now grind pepper and coriander without difficulty or pain. After all I purchased a $200 [[ASIN:B000A76VCY Breville 800CPXL Die-Cast Stainless-Steel Motorized Citrus Press]] just to reduce the hand stress I was experiencing with squeezing lemons and limes which I absolutely love and believe it was money well spent.

However, this pepper mill is not in the same league. I expected an elite "machine" that worked simply and well and here's what I got.

In the box is one large pepper mill that is mostly all motor. It comes with a small container of peppercorns and what looks like a square base on which the pepper mill should rest when not in use. (NOTE - It slips easily off this base if that is what it was designed for.) There are also 6 AAA batteries included.

The pepper mill has to be disassembled to load the peppercorns and also to extract the motor and load the batteries. Extracting the motor was incredibly cumbersome. There are 2 sliding levers on the inside plate that have to be shifted toward the inside of the motor with a pencil or file. In the process, my levers bent and almost broke off (so they are shoddy levers). Once the levers are no longer holding the motor in place, the unit has to be lightly shaken to dislodge the motor. It took a while for it to dislodge. Once the motor is removed, the batteries were easy to insert and the direction of insertion (negative and positive) were clearly marked.

After battery installation, I had to reverse the entire process. Inserting the motor is tricky as well as I had to line up certain parts, then push down the motor, and re-seat the levers out and under the base lip.

The top of the vessel holding the peppercorns that came with this product also acts also like funnel. I had to unscrew the top and punch out the center piece then lay this over the peppercorn reservoir to fill it. Once that was done. I screwed the holder to the base. (NOTE - Save the container that came with the peppercorns because it is a measuring cup for refilling the reservoir.)

As per the manual, only black, white, and green (dry) peppercorns of 5 mm (0.2") or less should be used in this mill for optimal performance. It also grinds pink peppercorns as long as the pink ones are no more than 15% of the peppercorns being ground. In addition, it grinds dry coriander seeds.

There are six (6) gradations of grind (from fine to coarse) marked on the bottom dial. Based on my tests (since the instructions are not clear on this), it appears the single horizontal line indicates a fine grind and as the lines increase in number to six (6) lines that indicates a coarser grind. The grind level is set by turning the dial to line up the desired grind lines with the letter P written on the reservoir (which is difficult to see).

To dispense the pepper, I just lightly touched the "button" on the top of the base to activate the motor. A light comes on and then dispenses the pepper according to the grind level set. The mill grinds quickly and well. Since the unit engages the motor easily, it means if one of my cats touches the top, the pepper will also grind.

In summary, had I paid for this product, I would have sent it back for a refund. The batteries are too difficult to get to, the levers holding the motor in place are poor quality and easily broken, there is no shutoff for the motor once the batteries are installed so the slightest touch of the button grinds pepper, and it does not feel like the elite "machine" I expected. Also, the lifetime warranty is on the motor only and no other part. If this grinder came with USB or other rechargeable and easy to insert batteries, had the ability to turn off the motor, felt like a quality kitchen tool, and the instructions were clearer (five languages follow each instruction) then I would have given this 5 stars. As it stands now, I consider this a working prototype only and not a kitchen tool that should be sold for such a high price.

Produces mild heat on highest setting; arrived with black smudges on top; initial use has heat smell. This deep pocket heated mattress pad for a king-sized bed is like a heating pad. There are two controls that plug in on the top of the mattress cover and have settings for warm, low, medium, and high heat. The warm setting is the default. I could not feel much heat from any of the settings except for the high setting. The high setting provided a very low and very nice warmth. There are two controls; one for each side of the bed. There is a slight heat smell during first use.

I have a king sized bed that has a tall mattress with a topper. I require 16" deep pockets and the pockets on this are large enough to handle that even though there is nothing on the packaging that says that. This cover works (longevity unknown) but the CONS make this a pass for me.

PROS
- It provides a nice light heat on the highest setting that apparently shuts off after 10 hours. I did not test the 10-hour shutoff as I'm rarely in bed for more than 6 hours.

- There are two controls for both sides of the bed so the other bed partner can select a different heat setting.

- The mattress pad is attractive and comfortable to lay on (except for the area with the plugs).

- It has deep pockets for a tall king-size mattress and fits up to my mattress pocket size of 16".

CONS
- The electrical connection should have been located on the headboard side of the pad and only on the rim (meaning pocket side) of the pad. Currently, the connection is located at the foot of the mattress pad (based on the label). Of course, I can turn the label upside down and face the connection toward the top (which is what I did to access an electric socket); however, the plug on both sides is on the top and can be felt as a lump if laying down in that area.

- The pad I received arrived with black smudges as if someone walked on the mattress pad. When I order a new product, I expect to receive it in pristine condition.

- There was some cotton sticking out of the trim (see photo). This is a minor detail and can just be cut off, but it is another sign of sloppiness.

- Although the elastic section (pockets) fit over my mattress, the elastic is not gripping enough. This means, it is easy for the mattress pad to slide off the mattress unless I sandwich the remaining cloth between the mattress and the box spring.

- There is a bit of a heat smell during first use; not much but is to be expected.

- This unit has to be unplugged daily as there is no shutoff except for the claim that it shuts off after 10 hours, which I did not test.

- I would not count on being able to wash this successfully. It says I can wash this in a machine for 5 min but I personally wouldn't do that. I would suggest spot cleaning if needed.

In summary, this mattress pad works to produce very low heat on the highest setting. It will fit a king-sized bed with 16" to perhaps 17" deep pockets but the elastic is too loose to keep it on the bed unless it is wedged between the mattress and box spring. The location of the plugs is a problem and the dirty topper I received is an utter disappointment. The current price of $33.99 ($39.99 minus 15%) is very reasonable for this. A mattress pad without any heat for a king-sized bed is usually priced much higher. My recommendation is to pass on this pad and buy flannel sheets for the winter that keep one warm and toasty under the blankets. If a heated mattress pad is desired, I would say to look elsewhere.

I have owned two of these microwave ovens. The first time, the doorlatch failed after 16 months â€“ four months beyond the warranty period. The second model just failed this week, four months after purchase. The problem was exactly the same both times â€“ a doorlatch that becomes increasingly difficult to engage when you close the door, finally failing entirely to engage. The result is that the microwave will not turn on no matter what you do.

I just did a broad Internet search, and I have learned that Panasonic microwaves of various models are absolutely plagued with door latch failure. Sites from Consumer Reports to Panasonic's own review site are all choked with complaints about precisely the kind of doorlatch failure I experienced twice.

It is astounding that Panasonic continues to manufacture microwaves with this faulty design. It is also astounding that Panasonic has never recalled its microwave doorlatches and replaced them at its own expense, regardless of warranty period (although this would likely be economically disastrous for the company, given how many of these defective devices is it has sold).

Both times I have owned this model, I have admired every aspect of its performance except for the fact that the lifespan of the model is measurable in months. A Panasonic microwave would be a good choice for you only if you are fine about replacing your microwave (or going through the hassle of a warranty repair, if you are lucky) at least once a year. I am now investigating commercial models. These have fewer bells and whistles, but are built for hard use and long life.

Good Quality Heater- Not as good as I was hoping. When my two 21 year old ceramic heaters started showing signs of failing I started hunting for new ones. After a long and arduous search I decided to give this one a try. I am very glad I did. We have a living room that is about 400 sq ft. that opens to both a sun room and the kitchen, about 900 sq ft total. This heater was able to keep the entire area in the upper 60s when it was below freezing outside, no sunshine. It took 1 hour to heat this area from 58 to 68. I do believe if this was utilized in a closed area of 400 to 500 sq ft., it would be more than adequate.

The construction is pure and simple. It uses a small blower similar to what is used in your furnace to distribute the heat. It is much quieter than fan driven heaters, has a higher cfm (cubic feet per minute) output and the delivery of the heat is very warm, and "softer" than fan driven models. It tends to make a sizable area around it feel cozy as best as I can describe it. When plugged in and turned on high it doesn't seem to have any more loading on the circuit than a standard hair dryer. It is much more efficient in producing and distributing 1500W worth of heating than anything I've ever seen.

The unit does remain cool to the touch except one small area above the heater core on top where you might describe it as barely warm. The filter on the back is basically a hair screen, not a dust filter. The power cord is 6 foot long, adequately sized, with a standard 3 prong outlet connection. The casters are adequate for hard flooring, not carpet. But the unit itself does not feel like it is over 20 lbs. to me. The remote is cute.

I'll be curious to see the electric bill. We are now successfully using this one 1500W heater to warm the same area it required two 1500W ceramics to heat previously. My only last concern would be with longevity. With a 3 year warranty I expect with normal care and maintenance (cleanings) this heater should be around a long time. I will update if I run into any problems.

UPDATE 2-17-2014: This unit is now failing. It still produces heat on the Lo setting, but produces much less on the Hi side then when new. Now the high and low side are producing an equal amount of heat. The unit has been subjected to no rough handling whatsoever. The filter has been cleaned exactly as recommended. I can only conclude that something inside the unit has failed. Considering this unit has a 3 year warranty and has displayed a failure within 4 months is quite irritating. I will be inquiring how much this would cost me to ship it back to the manufacturer for repairs, but no matter what the cost I find failure within this short of a time span pathetic, thus I have revised my rating on this product. With this kind of performance I could NOT RECOMMEND purchasing this product based on longevity.

Not for beginners.... THE GOOD:
--------------
* Seems like a high quality machine. Very well built
* Default is set to seal 95mm cups, but you get three extra adapters for 85 and 90mm cups.
* Heats up fairly fast, 3 minutes is the specification.

THE BAD:
-----------
* They don't seem to be targeting regular homeowners because the instructions are woefully inadequate. If you are in the business, or have used these machines before, I'm sure you'll be okay. For me, it was all trial and error, and based on my trial and error, here are questions newbies will have, which a manual should have addressed:

1. Orientation of the roller film. They do have a diagram that I followed, only to realize the seal was upside down. A youtube video help me get it right, which I will talk about below.
2. How long do I press the cup without burning it? You know why I realize this is a question that should be addressed? Because some of my cups came out burnt, plastic melted. Look at my picture. LOL!
3. How far do we crank the handle? At times I felt like I might be crushing the cup and the drinks will spill. Because no matter how hard I push, the film just wouldn't cut. It would only create a perforation. I then manually separate it. This may have something to do with the height of my cup versus the level of the base. You can use a screw driver to move the base up or down. I will have to trial and error with the height of the base to figure out if this is what's causing the issue.

You see what I mean? There should be a manual with operational advice, recommendations and tips. There is nothing. You are on your own, it is 100% trial and error to learn this machine. If you want to know how to put the roller film in property, search YT using this phrase.. "Cup Sealer Machine Unboxing Demo - Verly." You will get an unboxing demo by a guy name Zian Vlag. He uses a different model, but I can see the roller guides for the film are the same. By watching him, I then realized my film was upside down. I am sure this is a 5-Star machine, but without an operational manual, or even company videos, this is a 2-Star product overall.

****DO IT THIS WAY****

Building is from scratch!! Better for smaller shoes..!!. Wow! A bit intimidating when seeing the construction that must take place.. every section of PVC pipe comes in single sections and must be built one connector at a time!! Truly, a bit of a jigsaw puzzle so I recommend first spreading out and grouping all pieces into their matching counterparts. Next unroll one mesh “platform” at a time and insert pipe inside the mesh sleeves and cap with corners to create the physical platform- repeat for all 4 levels. Once you have shelf structure to work with.. it’s a lot more feasible to connect the layered tower. I’m assuming this is the reason for the lower price point.. The buyer does 100% of the construction- something to keep in mind when purchasing! If a PVC pipe tower is not in your wheelhouse.. another option maybe better.

Once assembled.. this has a lower height profile which helps keep it stable. This is definitely smaller in size and could be useful in tight or limited spaces. However, if using with adult size shoes…this more likely is to fit 6-8pair only (depending on the shoe.. some shelves may only fit 3 single shoes vs. 4…) I would definitely recommend this for children size shoes or, adults with smaller feet!

Overall, this is not for easiest purchase for convenience! It will take a bit of patience to assemble.. and once built it does have limited capacity. So, be certain it will fit your specific needs in its sizing and structure prior to ordering. I deducted a star for the intense building…(It would be nice to include in description this will come 100% unassembled- as that may make a big difference for some.. I can’t imagine my parents at their age trying to put something like this together?!!) and deducted a star bc, 2 adult pair of running shoes can’t fit on shelf- not in size 10mens. And it state this can hold 8-10… otherwise, this has merit for specific needs if they match this shoe racks capacity! I hope this info can help your decision.

Overall- for your price point this is best used as the duvet insert and not the finished top layer. Materials used are of good quality- its lacking in the finishing touches.. the touches that will help to give this longevity. Hoping this info can help your decision- stay safe and warm everyone!

Best for any venturing out on their own the 1st time!!. This is a 3 pack set of cutting boards sold for a price point under $15. This provides different options and will be quite useful for some. However, it’s not the best option for myself.

•Sizing is smaller then, bigger. The largest cutting board is just a bit bigger than a standard sheet of paper. Great for use in a boat galley, RV, dorm,1st time apartment, etc.. Bc, these have easy storage capability and on the smaller board- there is a gutter for any liquid runoff and debris.. handle on largest board has Hollow center and could be used to hang! These are some nice features and creature comforts to have but, its not conducive to my needs in my kitchen cooking for a family of 6.

• Smooth, round edges and low height make it difficult to pick up the smaller 2 boards as, they have no handle. I have to slide board to the edge of counter to get a grip underneath- depending on what I’m cutting it can be a bit tricky! Backside of board is smooth without rubber “stoppers” letting this slide around on counter. Not a good feature when trying to cut! I have to Tetris some counter items to hold cutting board still-

•2 wks. of using, I’m seeing knick's in the surface.. How?!! I’ve been extra cautious and used only a paring knife. I’m actually replacing a similar style cutting board I’ve had over a decade.. But as much as I need this, I’m worried this may not have the longevity to go the distance..?!

•Cleaning is KEY! be sure to do it right. Personally, I cut all meat on stone block.. and this keeps yuck and bacteria from sinking into wood grain or, a Knick or, cut on a plastic board. Keeping raw meat from Cross contamination with other food sources- use separate board for meat and always clean properly.

This is a great economical set of boards and good for light cooking or, extra cutting surfaces for food prep. It isn’t size I need for a larger family on daily basis- But, it could be a good starting board for those beginning to venture out in their own kitchen.. or, use in smaller places as listed above.

I hope this info helps… Feel free to let me know!

OK Serving Bowl for COLD Foods. If you are shopping for dishes for the first time in a while you’ll notice a plethora of dishes made of Melamine. The prices are reasonable and the design choices plentiful. As a potter who understands the dangers dishes can pose due to the glazes used, I decided to dig into what Melamine is and whether I wanted to use it with my family.

So let’s start with what exactly is Melamine?

Melamine is an organic compound also called urea or carbamide, that is mixed with formaldehyde to form a polymer resin. Melamine can also be mixed with other inorganic compounds to become a flame retardant, a fertilizer and a plasticizer for concrete.

Melamine is commonly used to make strong hard plastic dinnerware but is made using formaldehyde and the safety of melamine dishes is controversial.

Any heat can cause these chemicals and resins to migrate into your food, so it’s wise to stay away from plastic and melamine tableware options as they aren’t exactly the safest dishes to use for health.

Melamine plates are not oven safe and the FDA advises against using melamine in microwave ovens. Melamine is made from melamine-formaldehyde resin, and the melamine can contaminate food at 160°F and above.

Pfaltzgraff?

I decided to do a bit more digging... Like many, I have been eating off Pfaltzgraff dishes my entire life. I have the dishes my mom had that I then inherited - they are Pfaltzgraff dishes that have been in daily use for 45+ years.

Pfaltzgraff had been produced in Pennsylvania since 1811 with the first factory opening in 1865. Pfaltzgraff was truly an American standard that many of us knew, grew up with and the name carries weight.

In 2005 the Pfaltzgraff Co. was sold to Lifetime Brands, Inc. It was at this time the vast majority of production moved from the US to Mexico and China. After doing quite a bit of digging, from what I can decipher, of course this information is not easily found, it appears the Melamine lines are produced in China.

So My Thoughts on this Melamine Serving Bowl...

There is no question that it’s plastic. This will be a personal preference to some degree but I think plastic serving dishes look cheap. Yeah the outside looks like marble - kind of. It is lightweight and Melamine is harder to break than ceramic - though it will break, especially if it’s cold.

After extensively researching Melamine dish safety I’m not comfortable with the potential risk of chemical leaching when temperatures are over 160°F or if foods are acidic. These dishes are definitely not microwave or oven safe. Something I always have to keep in mind is that while I would know not to microwave anything within this bowl that doesn’t mean my son or a guest would know that.

This bowl is one that I store in a different cabinet and use when we are going to a pot luck and I want to take banana pudding or the like. It works ok for that, it washes well and looks nice. Beyond that type of use I would not recommend it.

Well-Made, Works Well, But Not Best Available Corn Stripper Tool. If it weren't so fiddly to use, I would really love this RSVP SHUCK DELUXE CORN STRIPPER. The product's clear plastic outer tube is both its best and its worst feature. The best, because the tube catches all of the stripped corn kernels, and is easy to empty. The worst, because the tube must be opened and closed for every single ear of corn; each ear of corn must be carefully positioned inside the tube; and the yellow cap at the bottom of the tube has screw threads that run in the "wrong" direction. (To unscrew something, the mantra is "righty tightey, lefty loosey"--but this tube opens when turned right, and closes when turned left. Probably it's designed this way so it won't unscrew when the corer is twisted.)

The stainless steel "corer" is sharp, and it cuts the kernels off the cob with very little downward pushing effort. However, it misses all the kernels at the narrow end of the ear. The gadget is a little confusing at first, but simple to use once you understand how it works. You cut the kernels off by twisting the scalloped yellow part that's attached to the stainless steel corer; then you use the knobbed yellow part to push the stripped cob out of the corer. It's easiest if you take the knobbed part out before you strip the corn kernels off the cob. All of the corn stripper parts are sturdy, and they are all dishwasher safe.

This RSVP Corn Stripper is slightly more efficient than my [[ASIN:B000V78JGO OXO Good Grips Corn Stripper]], which has to be emptied several times for each ear of corn, and is a bit awkward to take apart and reassemble each time. However, my favorite tool for this job is the [[ASIN:B006GDRD9G Zyliss Corn Stripper]], which strips an entire ear of corn completely with 4 or 5 quick downward strokes (when you hold an ear of corn over a bowl or plate, you don't need either a tube (RSVP) or a container (OXO) to catch the stripped kernels).

Because it's fiddly and not the best available tool for the job, I rate this well-made product at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

The display shows time in hours, minutes, and seconds-- the maximum time is 23 hours, 59 minutes, 59 seconds. The timer is powered by a single flat, round LR44 battery (included).

The timer's best feature is the independent memory function that will recall your most frequently used time setting. I keep the memory set at 20 minutes--the time it takes to freeze homemade ice cream--but the memory can be easily erased and reset to something different whenever you like. You do NOT have to set the timer and allow it to run to completion to invoke the memory function (a requirement with many other kitchen timers). Instead, the memory is set independently, by using the regular Hr.-Min.-Sec. buttons and then hitting the Memory button. The timer has a built-in stand, plus a fairly strong magnet that you can use to attach the device to any convenient metal surface.

I rate this timer at 5 stars ("I love it" on the official Amazon scale). The only negative thing I have to say about it, is that it is quite small. At 2" high by 2-5/8" wide, it is slightly smaller than a credit card. Because my household has two cooks, I use this timer alongside another excellent timer, the [[ASIN:B004PYA3B8 Robic Three Memory Timer]], which is limited to 99 minutes but which remembers three frequently used time settings.

“Plain Vanilla” Electric Alarm Clock Has Battery Backup System. Old habits die hard, so I like to have an electric alarm clock--one with an easy-to-set alarm--on my bedside table. Ths AMAZONBASICS DIGITAL ALARM CLOCK (with Large 1.4-Inch Display) satisfies that need. However, it seems expensive (about $18 on Amazon) for what it is--a simple electric alarm clock with a single beeper alarm.

The alarm clock does have one nice “extra” feature. It has a battery backup system that keeps the clock going during a power outage so that your alarm still wakes you up on time. The backup system requires a 9V battery (NOT included).

For a couple of dollars more (about $20 on Amazon), you can get an [[ASIN:B07DQYFCXM AmazonBasics Digital Clock Radio (FM only)]]. This alarm clock has two separate alarms, a battery backup system, an FM radio, and a USB charging port. The built-in radio speaker is pretty bad, but you can use the beeper alarm option instead. I think that the clock radio with two alarms is a better choice than this “plain vanilla” digital alarm clock.

High-Quality Travel Pillow Is Difficult to Bag. This HAOBAIMEI TRAVEL NECK PILLOW (Memory Foam, Grey) is a high-quality, well-made travel pillow that can be positioned in myriad ways to support your head/neck comfortably in all kinds of seating. However, it’s bulky--about the size of a small loaf of bread when bagged. The bagged pillow is also an awkward shape (and a little heavy) to carry everywhere you go.

The memory foam provides solid support. However, the pillow is much more difficult to bag than the product video suggests. Bagging requires hand strength and sitting down so you can force the folded pillow into the bag.

A bonus thin sleep mask is included, but it isn’t very effective in blocking out light. It’s just a flat piece of padded black satin fabric.

Expensive Specialized Crevice Tool. This BLACK & DECKER HHVJ320BMF26 SMARTECH CORDLESS 2.0Ah LITHIUM HAND VACUUM is a terrific crevice tool, but the price (about $122 on Amazon) blows me away. There are features that I love--the lighted display that shows how much charge is left; the built-in crevice tool extension--but the usefulness of this "hand vacuum" is severely limited by the 2-inch-wide nozzle. The battery holds enough charge to vacuum a flight of carpeted stairs on the high-speed "power boost" setting (impressive!), but it takes a zillion passes to do stairs in 2-inch-wide strips.

The suction is okay on the low-speed setting, and very good on the high-speed setting. It takes 5 hours for a full charge, so you'll probably want to store it in the plugged-in charger (wall-mounting hardware is included) to keep it topped off, as the manual recommends. The charger light turns off when charging is complete, but removing the device from the charger for even a few moments will cause the charger to restart for a few minutes.

The crevice tool extension makes this ideal for cleaning my stairway, which has a stair lift installed. (The support posts for the stair-lift track not only collect dust, but are hard to clean around.) However, the release button for the extension is stiff, so that it's often difficult to push the extension back into the nozzle for storage. The crevice tool extension is great for cleaning crevices in overstuffed furniture. The nozzle without the extension does a good job of dusting a smooth rubber floor mat.

The hand vacuum is fairly easy to clean. The big cyclonic element in the handle releases easily, and the whole thing pulls out sideways. Dust, dirt, and larger particles collect around the plastic filter module, and are easily dumped into a trash container. However, thick dust accumulates quickly on the cloth filter inside the plastic filter--and it clings, so the "dust bunnies" must be pulled off by hand. (This isn't good if you have allergies or asthma.) Filter reassembly is simple, and the filters are washable.

This is a vacuum for dry materials only. After washing, the filters need to be completely dry before you operate the vacuum. The cyclonic element is not particularly capacious, so I can't see this device as indispensable for ordinary kitchen cleanups like cereal, flour, or dry pet food spills. It is lightweight, and well-balanced for hand vacuuming.

As good as this device is for cleaning crevices in upholstered furniture and for cleaning carpeted steps, it is expensive for such a specialized tool. Also, it requires storage space and an electrical outlet to keep it charged and always available for ready use. For these reasons, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Well Designed, Light, Convenient, not the best on heavily soiled carpets. I have mixed feelings about this carpet cleaner.  I am spoiled by having used a Rug Doctor, which really does an excellent job.  My old Rug Doctor is on its last legs, so thought I would give this cleaner a try.  I had bought a Bissell carpet cleaner several years ago, but ended up returning it as it didn't work that well.  Thought I would try again as I assumed that improvements had been made over the years.  It does seem like it is a better machine than the one from several years ago and it really seemed to get a lot of dirt out of the carpet and pulled out a lot of lint too.  I would classify it as an adequate cleaner if your carpets are not heavily soiled.  It didn't work as well as my Rug Doctor to get out ground in dirt, but when you consider that it is 1/2 to a 1/3 of the price of a Rug Doctor, it does a lot for the price.  I like the idea that the tank you fill will hot water comes out and you can take it to the sink and leave the machine plugged in and not have to move it.  With my Rug Doctor, every time I need to fill the water, I have to unplug it and take the whole machine to the sink, dump the dirty water and fill it with clean water from a pitcher.  With the Bissell, you just run the water directly from the faucet into the tank.  The power cord is a reasonable length.  It's long enough so you don't have to move the machine too often, but short enough not to get in the way.  The machine is light and easy to manuveur. Rug Doctor uses one backwards pass to clean.  The Bissell uses one forward and one backward pass dispensing cleaning solution and then a foward and backward pass to vacuum up the water.  It's 4 passes instead of one, but the machine is not that heavy so it's not a big deal to make the 4 passes.  I liked the hand attachment that you use with the built-in hose; it worked very well.  The machine noise is about normal for a carpet cleaner, approximately like a vacuum cleaner.  Very easy to assemble the machine; just a few screws.  So what's wrong with this machine?  On heavily soiled carpets, it seemed to leave a lot of streaks and put out too much soapy mixture.  It's possible I used too much cleaning solution as the small included bottle said double strength, but I used the included measuring cup, so I assumed it was the right amount.  I also had a hard time figuring out how the built-in hose was supposed to wrap around; there is no picture or diagram.  My sister figured it out right away how to do it, so chalk that up to my being a dummy.  The biggest issue I had with this machine is that when you turn it off and start to move it, it drips a lot of water out and can spot up the carpet; then you have to run it again over the spots and they don't come out easily.  I also noticed that the restricted area that sucks up the water is narrow enough that lint accumulates and requires cleaning just about after each use.  This is a decent machine for the money and I would give it a solid 3 stars; maybe 3 1/2.  If you don't have a lot of very dirty carpet, this might be perfect for you.  It beats paying double or triple the price for a more heavy duty machine, unless you need the heavier duty cleaning power.  If you clean your carpet regularly, this should do the job just fine.  If you have a lot of dirt and have pets, this might not quite do the job, unless you use it often.
